text_fidelity_a:
Panasonic DMC-TS6A LUMIX WiFi Enabled Tough Adventure Camera (Blue) I’m a big fan of the Panasonic Lumix line of point and shoot cameras. I’ve been using one for years and, while it has limited features by today’s standards, it has yet to let me down. This latest one in the Lumix line offers a huge range of capabilities, provides outstanding image quality, but continues to suffer from a less than ideal user interface.

The camera comes with just the basics: the camera, a single battery, lanyard and a charger (plus manuals and software). I was a little disappointed right off the bat when I saw the charger. Unlike the older Lumix chargers that had a wall plug built into the charger than flipped out, this has a separate power cord. While that does make it easier to plug into the wall, it also means I have to remember to carry the cord with me to charge it.

Initial setup is straightforward, with the usual time/date setting. Since this has a GPS there’s also the need to go through initializing that option as well. All of these steps can be skipped, but you’ll be reminded to do so every time you power on the camera. It also displays a warning on screen about the waterproof limitations of the camera (and provides ample documentation as to what it can/can’t do re: underwater use).

The view screen is wonderful. Sharp, clear, and easy to read in all lightning conditions. The menu system will be familiar if you’ve ever used a Lumix camera but, if not, it’s still pretty straightforward. I still think Canon has the lead when it comes to having an intuitive point and shoot menu system, but Panasonic does a decent job. I like that with most options there’s a scrolling line of text that comes up to explain what the option is/does. That’s very helpful for options you don’t often use and need help with, but it does not interfere or slow down operation should you know exactly what you want to select.

I won’t list all the camera specs in this review since those are easily available in the listing and the Panasonic web site. Suffice it to say this offers a huge range of options and capabilities that cover pretty much any shooting situation. The Intelligent mode shooting scenario options (of which there are many) are helpful when you just want to point the camera and have it do everything else for you, including compensation for specialized lighting/scene situations. I especially like the macro option, which produced some impressive close-up shots that were sharply focused and clear even though I didn’t use a table-top tripod for stability but relied on the image stabilization features of the camera.

The video recording image quality is excellent good for a point and shoot cam. The performance of the built in mic is decent as well. This won’t compete with a dedicated HD cam, but for casual video shooting it’s a small, simple and easy to use setup that gets the job done pretty well.

The WiFi setup was surprisingly easy. I was dreading that since it often can be a bear, but this was quick and easy, and the included instructions were easy to follow. I use the WiFi option a lot since the USB port to connect to a PC is inside the camera (located under the battery compartment door). It’s done that way to maintain a water-tight shell, but is also means it can be hard to get to easily.

What has not been improved, and actually has slipped a bit, is the overall user interface (e.g., the buttons on the back). They continue to be small, hard to read, and don’t provide solid feedback that they have been pressed. Given that the camera is designed to be used in “rugged” conditions, larger buttons would have been a big plus, especially for zoom and the main menu keypad since those are used so often. Using the menu buttons is hard enough with bare hands; it’s impossible if you have gloves on.

I would certainly recommend this camera if you’re looking for a rugged point and shoot for outdoor use, but also if you’re looking for a high feature camera that never leaves the house. The performance and feature set are both excellent. The user interface brings my rating to four stars but performance and option-wise, this camera offers a lot for the price point.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic DMC-TS6A LUMIX WiFi Enabled Tough Adventure Camera (Blue)

Antennas Direct ClearStream 1MAX HDTV Antenna UHF VHF, Multi-Directional, 40+ Mile Range, UHD 4K, NEXTGEN TV – w/Adjustable Mounting Hardware (Black) Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

So far so good!
text_fidelity_b: Antennas Direct ClearStream 1MAX HDTV Antenna UHF VHF, Multi-Directional, 40+ Mile Range, UHD 4K, NEXTGEN TV – w/Adjustable Mounting Hardware (Black)

Razer Deathadder Infrared Gaming Mouse Okay, so Razer has a reputation for making products that are of low quality or break prematurely. There may be some truth to that. The "back" button double and triple clicks. I am going to replace the switch.

There is an LED lighted scroll wheel which feels of quality. The sides are a hard smooth plastic. The rest the body is coated with a rubber-like material. There is a lighted Razer logo and I turned off all the LED's.

Even though there is a problem with my mouse I decided to keep it and fix the problem. I have to say that this is probably the most ergonomic, comfortable mouse I have ever used. It has a very high arch and is shaped for a palm grip. I personally don't know if it would be a good gaming mouse ever. The sides are VERY slippery and if you needed a lot of control I don't know if you would have it. Especially if you had to lift off the mouse to readjust, it may slip. In my opinion the Roccat XTD Kone is the best mouse I have ever used. It is very big and heavy and there are grooves for your thumb and outer fingers. It feels more sturdy.

The reason I gave it 3 stars instead of 4, the mouse is always a little warm to the touch and it seems to absorb heat from your hand and get hotter. The Roccat mouse is made from similar materials and always feels cool. I have heard that there are parts of the circuitry that generate more heat than normal. So in summary, I like it for general use. If I was gaming or doing something that requires precision such as graphic design I would use the Roccat Kone XTD.

Edit: follow up- I have owned this mouse now for 3 weeks and I have it next to the Roccat mouse. I should share that I have used the Razer almost exclusively and switched to the Roccat only when I needed to use forward and back buttons (they are hard to reach on Razer). I think the Razer is more comfortable to rest your hand on for long periods at a time. However, it just seems that I have better control of the right click, left click, and forward-back buttons. The DA causes your hand to form an arch, while your hand is more flat with the Roccat. I wonder if your index finger is in a stronger postion with the Roccat; it feels so.
text_fidelity_b: Razer Deathadder Infrared Gaming Mouse

Sony RX100 IV 20.1 MP Premium Compact Digital Camera w/ 1-inch Sensor, 4K Movies and 40x Super Slow Motion HD DSCRX100M4/B Black I've said it a thousand times: "I think I could really get into (real) photography, but I just can't take another hobby that requires me carrying a whole bag of equipment across the world. If I get a DSLR, I won't take it to the places that I'd like to use it the most." Well...I think they made this camera just for me. I believe this camera to be capable of "real" pro photos, just the same as if I bought a DSLR and a single lens, which many people start by doing. It also makes a startup punk like me look like a pro, much to the chagrin of the real pros.

My other cameras include a DSC-H20, which is an older Sony model with a 10x zoom lens, multiple point-and-shoots, and a waterproof/shockproof Panasonic that I really like for my basic, worry-free shots.

My main question about this camera was, why does it appear to be Sony's flagship compact camera in every way, but yet it doesn't have the 30x optical zoom lens that some of the other Sony's have (or even the 10x of my DSC-H20)? I knew there would be an answer, but to find it, I had to start digging into camera specs, something I've been meaning to do for a while.

First, pro photographers tend to think that if you're using much zoom under most circumstances, then you're just being lazy. You need to get closer. In a landscape shot, zoom tends to flatten things out. I may have never noticed this, or WHY this is. You know, you go on vacation, take a lot of pictures, come back and some look great and others look bad. Maybe it's true that every time I zoom in on a landscape, I'm really just ruining my shot.

The other thing is aperture. Aperture basically tells you how clear the background of your picture will be versus your foreground (I'm just learning this myself, so camera pros, feel free to comment with better verbiage), a lower number being better if you want a totally clear picture, and the lowness of that number being what you use to compare the quality of lenses. It's also good to have a high end on the range because that allows you to take those artsy photos with something super clean up front and a blurry background. I've also seen some neat head shots taken that way, where even some hair starts becoming blurry.

Anyway, the low aperture on this camera is 1.8 all the way zoomed out, and 2.8 all the way zoomed in (you can set it as high as 11 in either case). This is a tight range with great numbers (notice that even here, you lose a little bit by using zoom). My camera with the 10x zoom has an aperture equal to 3.5 all the way out, similar to the 30x zoom cameras Sony has now. It makes a big difference, even to my amateur eye.

This camera, and my subsequent research, has allowed me to let go of the 10/30x zoom. Yes, those cameras are great, but this is the flagship mini for a reason. Now I understand. Just taking random pictures in my neighborhood, although so boring compared to my favorite International backgrounds, I can clearly see a quality difference.

The other main spec for cameras is shutter speed. This can be set for 1/32000 of a second all the way up to 30 seconds. The quickest shutter speeds will capture an instant in time without blur, while the slower ones will capture more action with some blur. They are also good for low light scenarios to expose the shot to more light. Very slow speeds should be used with a tripod or the camera set down someplace. This camera makes a noise (not an obnoxious one) when on auto and using a slower shutter speed, to keep you still. It's very intuitive and works well.

While you will get better shots than you ever had before using this camera on auto, the dial wheel allows you to set either aperture or shutter speed as a priority and leave the rest on auto, perfect for people that want to understand what a real camera can do, and who want to set up pro shots without yet knowing everything.

The controls on this thing are awesome. I love that there is no touchscreen to fight with and that everything is so intuitive. Great praise to Sony for knowing what fads aren't worth it. (One fad they did latch onto is that 180 degree rotating screen, which really is fantastically convenient and feels quite strong and well done). While we're talking about it, they also put in the fantastic viewfinder and the pop-up flash, which all completely recess into the body of this thing (an amazing work of engineering art).

Speaking of the flash, you won't use it often. Even on a cheap camera, I try to keep the flash off, but this thing does an amazing job of using ambient light for exposure (I believe this is the third pillar of photography). I swear, I have never seen such clear pictures in very low light. Instead of being grainy, I can pick up minute details (even zoom-able), and they appear brighter than the actual place they were taken. This, I believe, is because of the 1" image sensor they are touting. I'm impressed.

The 960fps thing. With only two seconds, this may be hard to set up the shot you want, but 2 seconds seems a lot longer in 960fps. Even just shaking your leg on camera, you'll see the odd aftereffects of your socks moving like you never did before. Stupid example, but that's the point: the details you get from 960fps slow-mo are amazing.

4k video. I really didn't care about all this until some guy at a conference pointed out how 4k has been used for pro video for years. Instead of multiple cameras to cover a hockey game, for example, you could just use one and zoom in on anything you want and still have high-def video. I realized we probably will move over to actually using it at some point. Well, here's your chance to actually use that 4k TV. It's awesome. It really is.

A note on SD cards. While most devices can read SDHC cards, which went up to 32GB, the reason they want you to have a SDXC card (which can be from 64GB to 2TB in theory) is because the speed ratings are higher. You need the speed rating of 3 (>100 Mbps) to really use these big data transfer functions. I suspect the 960fps is all that can be held in RAM, and that those speeds are way too fast for even the newest and best card (hence the 2 second limit on 960fps).

Suffice to say that I love this camera. I appreciate each of its mechanical and electrical features and how they're perfectly integrated to make this small, marvelous camera. Even in the leather case (not included), it's about the same size as my H20, certainly portable enough to have it when you want it, but with enough features and technology that you're not sacrificing anything in your photography.
text_fidelity_b: Sony RX100 IV 20.1 MP Premium Compact Digital Camera w/ 1-inch Sensor, 4K Movies and 40x Super Slow Motion HD DSCRX100M4/B Black

text_fidelity_a: Mediabridge™ HDMI Cable (6 Feet) Supports 4K@60Hz, High Speed, Hand-Tested, HDMI 2.0 Ready - UHD, 18Gbps, Audio Return Channel In past days I bought into a lot of the HYPE from non-manufacturer's like MONSTER CABLE that their overly expensive HDMI-ETC. cables including HDMI are worth the price. A digital signal especially for anything less than 25 orr 30 feet is a digital signal and as long as the cable is connected to the HDMI ends you get the same quality of 0/1 as you do with a ridiculously priced cable. I ordered both HDMI and Fiber Toslink cables from this branded manufacturer and they came packaged nicely and safely to prevent damage in transit with the UPS monsters and are performing perfectly. I actually did pay over $50.00 for a six-foot HDMI cable at Best Buy and all I can say is that I must have had a lot of money to waste as this brand is equally as reliable and I could have purchased twenty of these for the price of the one Monster at Best Buy. The only people who will argue these points are snobs who think there is some sort of prestige associated with having over priced digital cables. If this was for speakers or other copper reliant products I would at least partially agree that high-quality is very important but even there we are still getting products shipped mainly from China that have the fancy packaging and marketing hype attached to them and you can do a lot better shopping for solid quality without all the needless BS. But these and you will be pleased. SS
text_fidelity_b: Mediabridge™ HDMI Cable (6 Feet) Supports 4K@60Hz, High Speed, Hand-Tested, HDMI 2.0 Ready - UHD, 18Gbps, Audio Return Channel

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum RGB Tunable Gaming Mouse, 12,000 DPI On-The-Fly DPI Shifting, Personalized Weight and Balance Tuning with (5) 3.6g Weights, 11 Programmable Buttons I’m not a hardcore gamer anymore, so for the past few years, I’ve been using a Logitech M570 Wireless Trackball (thumb trackball). I like trackballs for everyday use, and it’s adequate for casual World of Warcraft playing. Most of the time I just futz around leveling alts or doing 5 mans with friends.

But lately I’ve been wanting a mouse I can customize, with more options to adjust my playstyle. It’s cold in my house in the winter, so I wanted to set up mouseover macros and use more mouse buttons, because my hands are cold sitting on the keyboard. So the G502 Proteus Spectrum seemed like a good mouse to review.

I just had one problem: my computer can’t customize the mouse. Why? I have a Mac Book Air.

Now, I know the G502 says on the box that it supports Windows. There’s no mention of Mac support. But I’ve never had a problem with my Mac recognizing Logitech mice, so I figured I’d be safe. What I didn’t know is that Logitech gaming mice have separate software from the Logitech Control Center for regular Logitech mice.

After some Googling, I found the Logitech Gaming Software, which supports Mac OS X 10.8.x and up. I installed it on a Mavericks machine and a Yosemite machine. Neither computer’s Logitech Gaming Software was able to find the mouse. The G502 Proteus CORE is supported, but not the G502 Proteus SPECTRUM.

So right now, I’m unable to customize any of the extra buttons or RGB lighting or any of the other special features. It’s a really fancy basic mouse. I will continue to check for Proteus Spectrum support in the Mac Logitech Gaming Center, and update this review when I can customize things. I’m going into so much detail on the Mac side of things because I know I’m not the only Mac person who tried to use this mouse. I think there’s a workaround with Bootcamp or using a Windows computer, but I’m unable to try that.

I did use the mouse for a few weeks, to test the comfort. I’m really picky on how mice feel in my hand. I’m female and have smaller hands. I like how this mouse didn’t feel too short, and it wasn’t too heavy or wide for me to use comfortably for hours at a time. I also liked the included weights, so you can adjust the weight of the mouse. I haven’t had a mouse with an adjustable weight before, and I liked that extra level of customization.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum RGB Tunable Gaming Mouse, 12,000 DPI On-The-Fly DPI Shifting, Personalized Weight and Balance Tuning with (5) 3.6g Weights, 11 Programmable Buttons

text_fidelity_a:
Corsair Vengeance 2000 Wireless 7.1 Gaming Headset (CA-9011115-NA) For the price, this is a decent set of gaming headphones. The build quality is perfectly fine for the price point. It doesn't feel as rock solid as more expensive brands, but feels like it will certainly stand up to normal usage.

The comfort is borderline. It feels fine for up to about an hour of usage, then the ear cups start to become somewhat uncomfortable and the headband pinches a bit. It's not the best set for hours and hours of usage, but for "normal" wear times I didn't have any problems.

The sound quality is quite good. Nice amount of bass response without sounding muddy. I also found it to have more than good enough sound quality for watching movies, with the dialogue coming through clearly. It's not the best for listening to music (the mid and upper ranges are a bit constrained) but for it's intended purpose of a gaming set, no complaints at all regarding sound quality.

My major problem was with range. I love the fact that these are wireless, but placement is critical. I'd lose the signal if I didn't vary much from a specific spot near the wireless adapter. Moving just a bit out of the "zone" killed the connection. That was a disappointment since, while I didn't expect to be able to roam around the house with them on, I did expect to be able to leave my chair and go a short distance without breaking the connection. No problems with signal strength when seated or within a few feet of the adapter, but hit and miss when moving more than a few feet away.

Other than the range issue, this is a pretty good value in a gaming headphone set.
text_fidelity_b: Corsair Vengeance 2000 Wireless 7.1 Gaming Headset (CA-9011115-NA)

I prefer a case that has a strap on the back for my hand and I like to use my iPad in vertical mode and onto horizontal. For that reason I have purchased an additional case that I use during those times.
Some features that would be nice for a future version of this product would be if when charging my iPad, it also somehow charged my keyboard. Another feature I would like would be if there was a touch pad mouse on the keyboard space. I find myself trying to use it like a laptop but that functionality isn’t there.
This laptop is high quality and feels like an actual keyboard, not a bad attempt like some iPad keyboards.
I like that I can control a lot of things directly from the keyboard like volume and Siri.
I’m very happy with this keyboard case.

Overall, the sound seems to be fine. HOWEVER, I have been wearing them all weekend and my ear canal HURTS. I have tried various placement in my ear canal and haven't found a good placement. So I am wondering, do I have these actually IN right?? Possibly not.
It would be useful if there was a clear demonstration on the proper placement of these devices. I almost returned them but decided to research more .. cause I don't want to go through the hassle of returning them.

The 2nd issue I have that I didn't notice is that the included buttons are iffy. They turn on and off OK but you have to press down on the button more than on my other ones that is just via touch. WHICH probably is a good thing as I would accidently fiddle with my other ear buds and it would turn them on and off and mess with them. THese you actually have a button.

The volume seems fiddly and doesn't seem to be working as well as I would like Again, they are buttons so you have to press down harder rather than just touching the device. That again, could be good or bad.
the other issue that may be the biggest problem is that there is not a forward 10 seconds or rewind 10 seconds. It is Next Track, previous track. That is less useful for me as I listen to podcasts rather than music. So Just something to consider. I may actually eventually replace these as I don't think they are perfect but I am hoping they will work for a bit more time until I can afford a better set for myself.

My only quibble is that I can't listen to the FM radio in stereo because the ear jack is for mono only. text_fidelity_a:
iHome 2-In-1 Pen Stylus for iPad/iPad 2 and all Touch Screen Devices (IH-IP2202) I expect that no one is going to use a stylus 100% of the time with their touch screen. There are, however, some times when a stylus is more convenient than using your finger. Drawing objects freehand is a common example. Another example is when you need to precisely move objects around the screen (eg in a CAD program) and this is difficult with your finger because your finger blocks your view of the target area.

There are many many touch screen stylus for sale on Amazon. Some cost less than 50 cents each. All the latest stylus have similar round soft touch rubber tips. All seem to work about the same. This iHome stylus doesn't seem to work any better than the others that I have tried.

The iHome stylus is better looking than most of the competition because of the long slim shape with silver-tone accents. Some of the cheap ones look very plasticy (though they do work just as well). Some other stylus are fatter, which makes them easier to grip if you have large hands.

The built-in ball-point pen is a feature that most other stylus do not have. The pen works well, though I do not know how easy ink refills will be to find. There is no literature in the package about what refills it can use.

Is this product worth $15? I have to say no, but I'm a cheapskate. You can decide on value for yourself, but look at the competition first.
text_fidelity_b: iHome 2-In-1 Pen Stylus for iPad/iPad 2 and all Touch Screen Devices (IH-IP2202)

GOgroove Computer Speaker Mini Soundbar - USB Powered PC Sound Bar with Easy Setup Wired AUX, Stereo Audio, Microphone Port, Volume Control Knob, Under Monitor Design for Desktop (Blackout) I bought this as an emergency when my parents' computer speaker went out. Based on the reviews it seemed like it would do the job and it seemed simple which is all we needed.

The connections are very simple and its a good looking speaker. Ideal for placing in that little space beneath a monitor in front of the stand. The headphone jack and manual volume dial is also a nice touch.

So everything up to the point of unboxing and connecting was great. Then we turned on the sound. It is tinny, there was no bass or even midrange body, and there was tons of distortion even at a modest volume. The best way I could characterize it is an old AM clock radio with a single speaker from the 70s. There wasn't anyway I could push decent volume out of these speakers and I tried every combination of source and speaker volume I could figure. If I was trying to use this on a laptop I wouldn't even bother. Better off with a cheap pair of computer speakers from Walmart.

Giving it two stars really because it does work, it had nice features, and it plays sound for very little money. But if you want better sound than what comes out of a cheap radio, spend a little more and get a lot more out of it. I can't imagine this speaker being useful in any way.
text_fidelity_b: GOgroove Computer Speaker Mini Soundbar - USB Powered PC Sound Bar with Easy Setup Wired AUX, Stereo Audio, Microphone Port, Volume Control Knob, Under Monitor Design for Desktop (Blackout)

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire HD 8.9", 8.9" HD display, 16 GB or 32 GB, Wi-Fi or Optional 4G LTE Wireless (Previous Generation - 2nd) As with the original Fire, the out of box experience is very nicely done. Very straightforward process of just turning it on and letting the tablet register and update itself. It took about 10 minutes (with the majority of the time waiting for an update to download) and it was ready to go. It picked up all my original Fire music and books from the cloud and most of my Fire apps. I was disappointed to see that a couple of my favorite apps (TED Talks and Play Music Videos Free) were judged not compatible with my new Fire. Hopefully updates will be coming soon.

The screen is delightful! Crisp and clear, and a marked increase in resolution versus the original Fire. Videos on the HD Fire are simply amazing.

The sound quality is also a marked improvement. While it was pretty much mandatory to hook up an external speaker for the original Fire, the new Fire puts out pretty decent sound quality all on its own. I still hook it up to external speakers (I'm partial to the Bose Companion 20) for movies and music when I'm at my desk, but it puts out more than adequate sound all on its own.

Response time is more snappy than the original Fire, and the carousel is easier to navigate (smoother scrolling). Picking up a WiFi signal seems to be better with the new fire - I'm getting all signal strength bars displayed in areas of the house where I could only get 2 or 3 bars with the original Fire.

The form factor is great for video watching. The extra screen size makes a big difference. The other huge advantage to the size is typing. It's MUCH easier to see and use the onscreen keyboard than on the original Fire. I had no problems typing without a stylus; on the original Fire a stylus is a must.

So far I don't see many misses other than a hard-to-find power button. The casing and build quality is not at the same level as an iPad, but neither is the price. I'm very pleased with the price-performance level of the HD Fire.

This is not replacing my original Fire - I'll continue to use that for most of my book reading and when I need portability. For everything else, the larger screen is well worth the additional cost.

I have a Nexus 7, the iPad 2 and an HP Touchpad and the Fire is my favorite by far. Not because either the original or this new Fire are the best in terms of build quality or speed or tech specs, but for one simple reason: the Fire makes it so incredibly easy to avail myself of entertainment and content. The tight link to the Amazon ecosystem is, for me, a huge plus - it keeps my entertainment pipeline full of things I want to read, listen to or watch with little or no effort on my part. And, best of all, a lot of that content is free through Prime.

Love it, and highly recommend.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire HD 8.9", 8.9" HD display, 16 GB or 32 GB, Wi-Fi or Optional 4G LTE Wireless (Previous Generation - 2nd)

text_fidelity_a:
Nuforce NE-700X Titanium Coated In-Ear Headphones - Aqua Silver Update after a couple of months

I still love 'em. Everything I put below still holds true. I rarely touch the EQ, and have been able to return to less processing is good processing listening.

One thing to add is that these are the first earbuds I could lay on my side with my head on the pillow and be comfortable. They have minimal strain relief but so far the cords have been perfect. I'd call tangle factor about medium.

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
Original review

So far I've tried
Skull Candy Titan - For me the best bass sound in this bunch. Tight punchy, accentuated but enjoyably so. Good for working out. But I value accurate bass above all. So I just use these for working out now.
Vsonic GR99 - very nice balanced sounding for $20ish dollars
Vsonic VC02 - Great sounding, but not a lot of bass. But what bass that was there was VERY good. My favorite phones in this list. But I kept losing the ear piece because of the removable wires. After the 2nd time I moved onto the VSD1
Vsonic VSD1 - nice sounding, if somewhat dry. It didn't make me get into my music, and I couldn't get them comfortable in my ears
Brainwaves S1 - These were my least favorite, boomy and not very comfortable, heavy thick wires. The only pair of the above I returned.

What they do well - assume anything not here is more than adequate

Presentation - I feel like I'm getting what the engineer was going for in the mix. More musical than any of the above without falling into a 'warm sound'. A nice mix of forgiving and accurate. Brightness right about where it should be.
Sound Stage - Airy, instruments well placed. Center image is not the strongest, but not lacking. Does a nice job of presenting the room acoustics/reverb in the mix.
Drums - Drums are rendered very well, better than any of the the above.
Cymbals - rendered very well, especially high hat. You can tell the cymbals are made of metal, and not just the tik-tik of the drum stick tip
Treble-sibilance - Close to perfect. Nice and bright without getting into hissy/tizzy. Vocal articulation is good.
Very easy to listen to for long periods of time. They are accurate without being piercing or harsh.
Sounded good right out of the box.

Misc sound notes - distorted electric guitar is just right. They respond to EQ very well, (which the Brainwavz did not do). I really notice when something comes into the mix even if it is soft. And louder things like guitar solos, really punch in the way you hear when mixing in the studio.

If I HAD to critique the sound (this is a review) there is a very-very, (did I mention very?) lack of something in the mids. Think chest/throat area of male vocals. But this is in the realm of sound signature, a matter of taste, not a deficiency and in no way lowers my enjoyment of these.

Build - wires are thin and flexible which is what I wanted. Very nice for wearing over the ear. Microphonics close to none whether worn up or down. No hearing foot steps or wire rubbing/bouncing on clothes. Light cord/cinch is great for running.
Shape - Bullet shaped what can I say, they are light and comfortable. I like the ring of rubber around them. It gives a little grip for inserting/removing them.
I LOVE that they have a red strain relief on the right side. No having to get my glasses to see some tiny R or L printed somewhere. Cord is nice and long, which is nice for using on a treadmill or elliptical trainer, or for wearing the cord under your shirt or down in a pocket.

As much as I liked the over all presentation and frequency response I feel I should point out these are not hella flat-accurate phones (like the VC02). If a true hi-fi sound, bright/accurate/revealing, is what you are after I'd look elsewhere (maybe the VC02) Don't get me wrong, since I used to be a sound engineer, and work on electric guitars, and have very accurate/bright/revealing/fatiguing speakers on my desk, I'm very picky about good accurate sound. But that makes these musical, easy to listen to for very long periods of time and poorly recorded and/or lower quality rips won't be hard to listen to.

The title says it all - the best I've tried yet and the first phones that made me stop 'shopping' for my next pair of phones.

Listening setup. Listening has been through an amp and separate dac connected to my computer playing 192kb - 320k - FLAC music, and through my old Droid Charge (I use this because I can enable the onboard DAC) and my Samsung Note II listening to ripped music (192k or better) or Spotify/Pandora at their highest quality settings available in the premium versions.
text_fidelity_b: Nuforce NE-700X Titanium Coated In-Ear Headphones - Aqua Silver

text_fidelity_a:
Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer) This is a really cool camera in a lot of ways, and yet there are two things about it that I hate:

1) It writes *.mov files. Why would any company choose that over so many great standards out there? Quicktime is the norm for *.mov files, with other players claiming to play them, but often with issues. Quicktime is one of those programs that - even after you uninstall it and delete everything you can find associated with it in your registry - will hound you until the end of your days to upgrade and constantly ask permission to take over your computer, will change other file extensions to play on it without asking, etc. Therefore, I so loathe Quicktime that I generally won't even touch an *.mov file.

I'd even be tempted to take the product down to three stars because of this, but there is some chance that this was the only format that would allow them to include the GPS data. I sort of doubt it because Apple (Quicktime) is the most ridiculously proprietary company I can think of, but I guess I need to give Contour the benefit of the doubt. Same benefit of the doubt used for annoyance #2:

2) You need to install more software to see the GPS data. I hate installing more and more software on my computer because everything installed is just another chance to have something running as a service or process all the time, wasting your resources. In general, all software is more "bloated" than ever these days, making our more powerful than before computers unable to perform better than before.

I also wish for some Blackberry support, but they might have some with BB OS 10, supposedly. Frankly, I'm not that interested in the smart phone features; they just slow you down.

As I said, the camera is really cool, though, for its ease of use and its mounts. It's obviously geared toward adventurers and people that want to roll off roofs in shopping carts like that one show that used to be popular. It has a great feel to it in its construction and durability, but I want to make clear the very big caveat that these are the only reasons you want this camera. Besides the annoyances mentioned above, I have a couple point and shoot cameras that do 1080p video just as well (actually better, given their native formats) and they are smaller and cost less. But it is pretty awesome to mount this on your bike for those "just in case" scenarios.
text_fidelity_b: Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
Canon PowerShot SD1100IS 8MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom (Blue) (OLD MODEL) This is a solid little camera that can provide excellent image quality under the right conditions. But it has two glaring deficiencies:

1. No fill flash option in auto mode. (There is a fill flash option in manual mode, but it's not easy for the casual user to find.) There's red-eye reduction, of course, and you can turn the flash off completely or let the camera decide when to fire it. But with the camera in auto mode, you can't tell it to fire the flash on every shot, regardless of what its sensor thinks. Major bummer when you want to photograph a backlit subject.

2. Shot-to-shot time is agonizingly slow, and focus time isn't especially speedy, either. This is a problem when, for example, you want to catch quick snaps of the animals you see on Disney World's Kilimanjaro Safaris. Ask me how I know.

I'm sure this is a fine camera for people who want to photograph landscapes, still lifes, and posed portraits. For candid shots of subjects in motion, it's not so great.
text_fidelity_b: Canon PowerShot SD1100IS 8MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom (Blue) (OLD MODEL)

text_fidelity_a:
Sony ICFC218 Dream Machine Clock Radio (Black) This is not a bad clock radio for the price I paid. It's not a great one either, but it fit the profile of what I wanted with one exception, which I'll get to in a bit.

First off, it's smallish, which is a blessing on a crowded nightstand. The display seems fine to me, neither too bright, nor too dim. It's easy to program, thank goodness. I've had a lot of electronics that require three hands, and a stopwatch to be properly programmed. The ICF-C218 has a button or a dial for each function. Just follow the instructions and you'll be fine. It's a bit hard to see the radio dial unless you pick it up, but that's a minor thing for someone like me, who pretty much keeps it on one station. It's not programmable; you have to change the station with a tuning dial. However the reception is excellent, even without an external antenna.

My quibble, and it's a relatively small one, is that the sound is tinny. I don't expect a lot out of a small radio like this, but I have a Sangean which is even smaller, and the sound is much better. It's not a deal-breaker, I got what I wanted in every other respect.

Bottom line: Good price point for a basic clock radio with excellent reception, and so-so sound.
text_fidelity_b: Sony ICFC218 Dream Machine Clock Radio (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
VIDBOX Video Conversion Suite Time takes a toll on al things. but memories captured on old vhs, beta and 8mmm film need not be lost forever. This product presents an easy and fairly fool proof way to convert them to a more contemporary format. Set upt is easy. Use the included CD to install the software and driver. Then attach the the color coded cables to the vidbox, then the computer and then finally connect to your VCR, camcorder or other device. You then select your connector, settings and record You can review, burn to a dvd or publish if you desire. The menus are easy to follow and the process is simple overall. while this product converts and stores it does not improve the quality. The end product is a duplicate of the original.

My mother has boxes of old tapes and the like and we are converting them. She is in her mid eighties and is finding the process an enjoyable way to revisit happy occasions. It is turning out to be a fun project. So in the final analysis, a good product that does what it says.
text_fidelity_b: VIDBOX Video Conversion Suite

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Zen X-Fi 8 GB Video MP3 Player with Built-In Speaker (Black/Silver) Zen X-Fi 16GB review 2-28-09

Had the Zen X-Fi 16GB for two months of daily use now.

The device is well built and solid. It needs a silicon skin for protection, though. That is extra but highly recommended so your expensive player doesn't slip out of your pocket.

First, the buttons are too flat and are not illuminated. Sounds like a small thing, but flat black metal buttons against a black metal background in the car at night are very difficult to find and press. If the buttons were transparent and had the tiniest LED behind them, they would be a lot easier to manipulate accurately.

No Bluetooth--I'm getting very tired of wired connection to my car and headphones. LOSE THE WIRES, Creative! The earphones that come with the Zen are terrific. Really good quality. But the wires are tiresome.

Though I'd rather have Bluetooth, Zen is Wi-Fi capable. You can wirelessly hook to your computer's wireless router and play or copy files back and forth, but it's so frustrating to make it function it's virtually useless. USB cable is the way to connect.

As part of Wi-Fi, Creative does provide something called "Media Server" that you can access via your internet connection wireless router if you're in range and properly connected. After waiting a couple of minutes for the connection to be made, you can listen to propaganda from all kinds of politically correct content like NPR, the BBC, Australia's ABC and KCRW. Yes, master: I hear and obey. Mostly a waste as you can't really select content you want, only what they supply. Definitely politically correct. And boring.

It has a kind of chat texting capability but that's what phones are for these days and the Zen's dinky keyboard just doesn't cut it. The keyboard is laid out the way it is so it can emulate a phone keypad when you're in chat mode. Too frustrating to use. It's why QWERTY keyboards are on phones now.

Bookmarks. A few minutes after being shut off, the Zen forgets where you were when you shut down. If you fire it up an hour after shutdown or dock it to your computer to upload new content, it starts playing the last file you opened from the beginning. This is a bit frustrating when you're part way through a three hour podcast. So Creative allows you to set a Bookmark from within the file you are playing. It's quick and easy once you figure it out. I use it all the time now. This allows you to set a point in a podcast so you can return to it later. But while you can set the bookmark from within the file, you have to navigate to the Bookmarks screen to select the bookmark when playing back later. Not very intuitive. Took me two months to realize the usefulness of the feature. Why doesn't it simply remember where I stopped listening by itself? My DVR does. Just resume from where I left off. But no.

The lower left button is programmable. It's called My Shortcut. You pick from a list of available functions and set it. This allows you to go to a particular favorite screen or function once you decide what that is.

The Zen first and foremost is marketed as a video and MP3 player. What I wish it could do is have a "skip forward" ability (again, like my DVR does) that allows me to skip forward 30 seconds or a minute (or a user defined amount) so I can move forward in predictable amounts instead of holding the fast forward button down. If it's going to be called a "player" of any sort, it should have a variety of player controls. Skip forward/back should be available. Firmware upgrade wish, Creative.

Speaking of the fast forward button, the longer you hold it, the faster it goes. It starts by forwarding at a slow rate, then speeds up until you are jumping forward minutes at a time. This is good for zooming to a point quickly. But if you want to go forward, say, seven minutes, holding the FFwd button down too long will launch it into hyperdrive and you'll be at 10 minutes or more into the file, then have to rewind/search back. Somewhat of a pain. No. A real pain. Let me skip forward or back in 30 second increments.

A great feature is its built-in speaker. It sounds like my transistor radio from my childhood. This feature was the main reason I bought the Zen: you don't have to use earphones if you don't want to. It is a great and rare feature among MP3 players. A pocketable mini boombox.

Creative's Centrale "iTunes wannabe" software is dreadful. I tried it for awhile, then uninstalled it and now just drag files to the device.

Video screen quality is very good but 320x240 is still a bit small. Diagonally it's 2-1/2"; 2" wide x 1-5/8" high. It's also the old 4:3 aspect ratio, not the modern 16:9. If you're viewing a 16:9 video letterboxed, you are looking at one tiny video.

The video player (as opposed to the music player) is very weak. Windows Media Player 11 it ain't. Another key reason I bought the Zen is because it promised it could play a plethora of video formats. Wrong. I have dozens of wmv video files which exist in many sizes and bitrates from thumbnails to HD. Unfortunately, almost all of them need to be converted via Creative's stand-alone converter app or Centrale into squeezed-down bitrates and 320x240 size. This process is clumsy and slow.

If virtually every file needs to be converted in order to play, it's not really playing the advertised list of formats: it's playing the format Creative has selected and must be converted to. Often, even if I render out a wmv directly from my video editing software to Creative's parameters, it still won't play properly without conversion. Yet another marketing promise dashed to pieces.

The Zen allows me to delete files directly from the Zen if I want to (as opposed to needing to plug into iTunes to delete or add). This is good.

It has a built in mic and audio recording capability and you can program the "My Shortcut" button to start the recording process immediately so you don't have to navigate to the recorder's controls.

It has an FM radio that only works if the ear phones are plugged in because the wire becomes the antenna. What I'd really like is an AM radio, though, for news, talk radio, traffic and weather. Who needs FM? That's what your MP3's are for in the first place, right?

The unit has an SD card slot, but it's not well integrated. Content on the SD card does not appear in the normal file list. You must navigate to the card and browse it separately. Worse, when you do that, it comes back with "There are no playable files in this folder" even when I know I put mp3 files on the card that the player can play. You have to use the "Import" function to move files from the SD card to the player's memory in order to play them. Think of the SD card as an aux thumb drive, not as expanded memory, except it doesn't even work like that, actually. If you think you can buy the 16GB and "double" its memory capacity with a card, think again. It's more of a gimmick than a useful feature. More Creative fluff that is long on promise but short on delivery.

By the way, when you plug the Zen into your computer's USB cable the Zen does not mount as a drive (what Windows calls a "Local Disk.") It "docks" as a "Portable Media Player" according to Type in Windows Explorer. This means you can't play directly from the player. If you click on a file on the Zen from within Windows, it moves the file to a temp folder on your C: drive before playing. Not a big deal, but if you intend on connecting the Zen to a USB input on your car stereo or computer, I don't think your stereo will be able to see the Zen's contents. While the Zen is docked to the computer, all the play buttons are disabled and the display indicates "Docked" until you unplug the device. On the other hand, you don't have to unmount the device. Just pull from the USB and go.

Poor Creative. Always trying. Never quite getting there. Won't be long now and a phone will do it all. Look at Sony Erickson's W760, iPhone or Palm Pre.
text_fidelity_b: Creative Zen X-Fi 8 GB Video MP3 Player with Built-In Speaker (Black/Silver)

text_fidelity_a:
House of Marley Uprise: Wireless Earphones with Microphone, Bluetooth Connectivity, 8 Hours of Playtime, and Sustainable Materials (Teal) I have a lot of styles of headphones, and I now know what this type is perfect for: exercising. Maybe you and everyone else already knew this. But if I'm running (or elliptical-ing), regular ear buds may fall out, and bigger headphones can fall off or at least get uncomfortable sweaty. Obviously, you don't want a cord connected to your phone for exercising, so these hit the sweet spot in all those ways.

They are very comfortable as well. The ear pieces that come connected are a perfect fit for my ears, and already offer real sound-proofing from the outside world (warning: you may appear to be an annoying millennial if you walk around isolated from the world with these all the time). They are comfortable, and I love the easy way that the ear-hanger pieces are removable. I also like that you can tighten up the connecting strap. There must be a cable in there, so I hope it doesn't wear out this way, but it seems to be pretty durable, so I guess it will be okay.

Actually, these are great. The charging area is barely large enough for the micro-USB port, but the battery lasts for quite a few hours. Not as long as some headphones, but the low weight is key here.

Also good for: watching movies or listening to music on planes if you have your own device. No cord to slow you down when a seat-mate wants to get past you, and they're comfortable enough to fall asleep in, unlike over-the-head headphones.

Oh, I saw a review that said the bass was poor. I do not agree. Music sounds great in these. They can operate on low power because they are so far up in your ear. Be careful to keep them at a reasonable level.

I would recommend these to friends.
text_fidelity_b: House of Marley Uprise: Wireless Earphones with Microphone, Bluetooth Connectivity, 8 Hours of Playtime, and Sustainable Materials (Teal)

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Zen Sleek Photo 20 GB Multimedia Player (Aluminum/White) I was in the market for a hard drive-based music player and didn't want to go the normal iPxx route, so I began checking into different brands. I had a list of criteria that the player had to meet:

-EXCELLENT SOUND. This is critical. A SnR (Signal to Noise Ratio) of 95db or better

-Excellent battery life. At least 15 hours

-At least 20 GB

-A color screen

-Sturdy build

-As little touch-sensitive controlling as possible. Click wheels are inaccurate and bothersome.

-Ease of use. Drag and drop is preferred.

-AC adapter for charging on the road or from an AC converter in a car

This player meets all of those needs. The SnR is 97db, I've gotten 18 hours out of the battery (remember that increased settings like equalizers and higher bitrates mean lower battery life for ALL players), the case is solid and brushed aluminum, the screen is pretty and quite sharp, only one touch-sensitive control is present, the player CAN drag and drop through Win XP, and it comes with a wall adapter.

I love the powerful sound this puts out and it can drive my big headphones with no problem. It can, like most HDD players, set aside a partition for storage. It has a good FM tuner, recording of FM and a little mic for voice notes. It can even sync with Outlook for contacts and other info. The hard disk seems fast and

Now for the drawbacks:

-You can't watch 15fps video on a tiny screen and reduce your battery life by 67%

-The USB cable is proprietary...no mini USB!

-The wall charger cable plugs into the USB cable...this means two cables for recharging from the wall

-Looking at photos and playing music at the same time is not possible

-Creative software is always iffy. Thankfully, in Win XP, you can open the player from My Computer and access its contents directly with non-DRM music and photos.

-Battery is NON-USER REPLACEABLE. This is odd for Creative.

-No mention of this on the Creative website. Thankfully, updated drivers ARE available from support.

This player would have been state-of-the-art about a year ago, but has been eclipsed by its bigger brother the Zen Vision with 30 and 60GB drives and video...however, if you're not buying into the "kill your eyes with tiny video on tiny screens" and just want a SOLID and RELIABLE player with booming sound, this is it!!! You can tell it's custom-made for Windows (it's MTP, not UMS for any computer), but if you're running XP, then it's a solid choice because you can skip the Creative software and just load music on it.

If you can get it on sale like I did, snatch it up. This is a little gem of a player!
text_fidelity_b: Creative Zen Sleek Photo 20 GB Multimedia Player (Aluminum/White)

The most important things are to work clean and work fast!  You have to thoroughly clean the surface - I use some water and microfiber cloth.  There must be NO dust at all on the screen, use some canned air if you need.  Lay down the sticky film by carefully lining up the hole with the home button and make sure the bottom edge is level.  Then work efficiently and briskly at applying the film from bottom up.  When I applied I got a couple little bubbles; as long as they are just air bubbles you can always work them out to the edge.  If you got dust trapped in there, they will be more or less permanent bubbles.  Work cleanly and efficiently and you should have a nice invisible shield on your ipad in no time!

text_fidelity_a:
Belkin VideoLink 3 Powerline Internet Adapter This seemed to be the perfect solution to a problem I was having with obtaining Internet access in my basement. The router is located on the upper floor of the house and, while access is fine in every room above ground, access in the basement has been minimal at best.

Installation was very straightforward - just plug one adapter into the router, the other into the wall socket, and plug in whatever device needs access into one of the three plugs located on the wall socket device.

Overall it works pretty well, but is highly sensitive to noise or heavy draws on the power line. For example, I have a dehumidifier in the basement. When that kicks on, I lose the connection. Sometimes it is regained all by itself, but most of the time I have to either reboot (or power cycle) the device that is plugged in, or unplug and then re-plug the adapter. I tried moving the dehumidifier to a different circuit than the one used by the powerline adapter, and also tried plugging the dehumidifier into a surge protector - no difference. So, I make sure the dehumidifier is off before I use any Internet device.

I've had the same issue with other appliances such as certain vacuums - turn them on, and the connection is lost. There have been no problems with appliances operating in other areas of the house, such as the microwave, laser printers, etc. Just happens when you use the appliance in the same room as the powerline adapter.

But, other than these powerline induced interruptions, the device works well. Speedy connection - can't tell any difference between this and any other WiFi connected device. Well worth taking a look at if you have some WiFi dead zones in your house. Just keep an eye out for someone who is about to use a vacuum when you're at a critical spot in the movie you're streaming!
text_fidelity_b: Belkin VideoLink 3 Powerline Internet Adapter

text_fidelity_a:
Netgear WiFi Dual Band Gigabit Router (WNDR4500-100NAS) Comp: iMac 27inch 2012, Mountain Lion

Installation: easy as 1, 2, 3. It does not get much easier than the install for this router. Working in minutes. Plug in lan cable from router to modem, power on modem, power on router, wait 1 minute (2.4ghz led is lit) turn on web browser. Web browser auto-opens to a simple, SIMPLE, web layout for the routers settings. DONE.

Speed: Excellent speed. Increased speed from an older lynksys router, web pages are opening with noticable % speed increases (as expected from this router)

Range: 5ghz. Router installed on a 2nd floor of 2flr 3200 sq ft home. Installed in 2nd flr bedroom at front of house, ONTOP of computer/work desk. Not ideal placement for the house, but has to be there for now. The dead pockets where signal dropped off on both floors before are now FULL signal. Places like the kitchen and other bedrooms receive FULL signal where solid walls and other electronics are placed. Areas that got marginal or no signal are now are now solid.

Other Equipment: 2 iPhones, 1 macbook, 1 Airport Express (client mode) - full signal strength and speed. Whereas the iPhones would drop in and out of 3G/wifi - they are now solid wifi in all areas of home. Macbook is flying with full strength. Airport Express has not dropped out, at all, like it used to, and seems to be 100% functional.

Conclusion: Cant say enough good things. Price is right, performance is excellent, and range, subjectively, has increased substantially to cover a 3200 sq ft home with the router on the 2nd floor. The ease of installation is fantastic. The pre-set router Network ID & Passwords make this router secure from opening the box and setting up (and easy to change) for those that are looking for security but might not have the know-how or are scared of 'messing up' the newtork.

Great product.
text_fidelity_b: Netgear WiFi Dual Band Gigabit Router (WNDR4500-100NAS)

Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Keyboard for Business (5KV-00001 ) I bought one of these 9 years ago and got a lot of use out of it. Yeah, the letters all wore off very quickly but I know where the keys are so no big deal. But it was finally time for a new one. The material on the palm rest was wearing out, etc.

I unpacked it and noticed it feels cheaper, oh well, not the first manufacture to make a product from cheaper materials as time goes on...

But the strangest thing... the little nubs you use to position your fingers are on the wrong keys??? On the left hand, it's under your index finger on the F key as expected. But on the right hand, it's under my middle finger on the K key. Makes no sense to have them be under different fingers. The middle finger, index finger I don't care but make it the same on both sides.

I already threw my old one out, and I could get it out of the trash but I tossed the dongle in the trash too would never be able to find it again...

The keys feel is Ok I'm not that fussy about key feel click, etc. but be warned that the communication on this keyboard with the dongle is terrible. It was bad on my original one and it's bad on this one. I was hoping there would be an improvement on that in the 9 years that I had the original.

In the end, unless there is something you really like about this keyboard (for me it was an ergo keyboard with no number pad) I would consider something else.
text_fidelity_b: Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Keyboard for Business (5KV-00001 )

Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th) “I wonder how long it has been we readers have gazed at the young person sitting under a tree at night reading a book on the Kindle home screen..oh, our love affair with books and being able to read our stories late into the night…...by candlelight….anywhere.”

Pre-release technology reviewers commenting on the price of the Kindle Oasis are wrong. The new Kindle Oasis is worth the the price Amazon is charging, including cover it hardly represents at all an increase in price when compared with a Kindle Voyage with cover. Yet it provides the two most asked for improvements in mobile devices: increased battery life reducing the need to frequently recharge, and improved screen legibility (new sans-serif Ember font, and more LEDS that provide increased brightness).

“When we are immersed into the story of our favorite books, only that world matters.”

Pre-release technology reviewers have compared the Kindle as a single purpose e-reader, to multipurpose devices like in smartphones, tablets and computers. When we choose to read, we are seeking a bit of solitude in the day and night. Oh, how easy it is to remember being annoyed with yet another incoming phone call, text message or email. The power of focus!

“The tactile feel of a book”

Pre-release technology reviewer have labelled the Kindle as luxurious with it’s leather cover. How soon we forget our books covered with leather! And we are willing to pay an extra price for it!

As I sit across the street from the one and only Amazon retail store “in the world”, I have unboxed and set up my new Kindle Oasis. Maybe I am one of the few ordinary people outside of Amazon and the technology press in the world to have been able to purchase one so soon. The feeling reminds me of going to a release party in the same shopping center for the latest Harry Potter novel.

This Kindle is new, like the latest release from our favorite author.

It connects me to reading anywhere, late at night when there is little light.

The Kindle Oasis is magical.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th)

text_fidelity_a:
Blink Outdoor Camera Wall Mount Bracket, Hard Protective Case and Metal Mount for Blink XT2 Cameras Weather Proof Adjustable Indoor Outdoor Mount and Cover for Blink Home Security(3 Pack, Black) When I installed my Blink XT2, I found I needed to move it a little lower so I could maybe see the face of the delivery person. Thinking I could unscrew the mount without removing the camera, I turned the camera to one side so I could access the screws. The camera fell to the floor. A little bit of friction is not sufficient to hold these cameras. That is when I started looking at these mounts which SHOULD be included in the box.

This is in several parts. Plastic camera-enclosing parts are held together with 4 small screws. The metal part is attached to the wall with 3 flat-head #6 screws.

Unscrew the adjusting part so the base of the mount can be attached to the wall. Do not try to adjust the angle unless this part is loose. Use care when tightening the screws - do it manually so the screws are not over-tightened. The aluminum base could be cracked by over-tightening.

The small screws that are used to attach the back cover to the front should be machine screws, and the posts into which they are screwed should be metal. This is my opinion and is because these screws will have to be removed and reinstalled every time the batteries are replaced.

One piece of plastic had a small 'tab' on it that had to be cut off before the back cover would attach to the front.

A hole in the bottom of the plastic is there to allow a charging cable to be attached. If you do not plan to use rechargeable batteries and have no need for the USB cable, plug the hole so insects do not go inside looking for a new home. I used a small piece of closed cell foam packing material (photo).

If you want to use these mounts with the earlier Blink cameras, you might want to use some foam so the camera does not move around inside the enclosure (photo).
text_fidelity_b: Blink Outdoor Camera Wall Mount Bracket, Hard Protective Case and Metal Mount for Blink XT2 Cameras Weather Proof Adjustable Indoor Outdoor Mount and Cover for Blink Home Security(3 Pack, Black)

text_fidelity_a:
NVIDIA Shield TV | 4K HDR Streaming Media Player The world's first all-in-one Plex box, the Shield comes w/ an unlockable (free) Plex Server inside --and not just another client/player like all other consoles. For those of us w/ a LOT of media, Plex is the pinnacle of enjoying your own media with the best interface possible (and it's free); whereas KODI is the best way for streaming media from the internet. The Shield recognized my old archives instantly, and also when I plugged in a USB3 SanDisk flash drive for extra space. I've had 3 WDTVs, 2 Nexus Players, and 1 MiBox, and I wasted all of that time and money until I got this. I've KODI Phoenix and Exodus for internet streaming, and Plex for my 200 movies, 25 seasons of TV shows, 75 instructional videos (on guitar, magic, and yoga), 6k songs, and all my family albums and artwork. I have the Plex client (player) for TV, phones/tablets, XBox 360, Chromebooks, and Chromebox.

The Shield has BOTH the Play Store and the NVidia Store on its dashboard. I can play all my games again because this console doesn't stutter and freeze up. I'd missed my Asphalt 8 when the others just couldn't handle the workload anymore. I can get even better games from the NVidia Store that the Play Sore doesn't have. Of course, all previous purchases come right back to the Shield --like the HomeRun HD. Plex has a deal they're making w/ HomeRun HD to possibly turn the shield into also doing DVR.

The gamepad has been totally redesigned and has gone from an Ugly Duckling to being prettier than a pail full of kittens. The hex-grip feels good in the hand for shooting zombies or driving on racetracks. The gamepad is rechargeable (yay!) and even comes w/ it's own charging cable. The once $50-extra remote is now included w/ the console. Like the gamepad, the remote also has a headphone jack for discreet listening and a touchscreen volume control and Mute.

These headphones are a grown-up Razer product, probably meant to be headphones you can take anywhere and not stick out as a gamer.

The Midnight Blue color is a nice change from black. I have a few pairs of wireless headphones and every single pair is black, so I appreciate having a little variety. Midnight Blue is a very deep blue -- so deep it’s almost black.

I’ve been trying the Opus headphones out for a few weeks and they have become the headphones I use every day. Before, I was using the Sony XB900N.

My favorite thing about the Opus headphones is how comfortable they are. The headband and ear cups have cushy padding. The headphones don’t squeeze my head too tight and don’t weigh a lot. I can wear these for 5+ hours at a time and not get a headache.

Sound quality is decent. I mostly use the Opus for listening to music and TV/movies. Compared to Razer’s gaming headsets, this isn’t one I’d pick for serious gaming. There is a tiny bit of lag and the low, deep sounds aren’t as punchy as with say, a Razer Kraken headset.

Razer’s claim of up to 25 hours of battery life seems pretty accurate. I didn’t keep a log every time I used the headphones, but I was able to use them for 4-5 hours a day for a good week before needing to charge. Unfortunately there is no battery indicator on the headphones to know when the battery is running low.

I don’t love the Razer Opus app needed to tweak a few of the settings. I have an older Android phone running Nougat, the app is incompatible with my phone. So I had to borrow my mom’s iPhone to install the app. By default, the headphones shut off after 5 minutes and I could only change this setting in the app. The app also allows you to switch between a few audio presets (but you can’t create your own) and check battery life.

If I take the headphones off my head, they automatically pause whatever I’m watching or listening to. I like this; my mom often talks to me when I’m wearing headphones, so it’s a lot quicker to just take them off and now I don’t have to manually pause. This is a setting that can be changed in the app.

The Active Noise Cancelling is what I expect for a pair of headphones in this price range. It’s decent. Not great, not horrible, but good enough to mute most background noise. But I don’t like that there’s not a light or indicator on the headphones to tell when I have ANC turned on.

The Opus doesn’t support Bluetooth multipoint.

The headphones charge via USB-C. The included case stores the headphones, charging cable, USB-C to USB A adapter, 3.5 mm audio cable, and airline adapter. The case actually has an outline on the bottom to tell you how to fit the headphones inside.
text_fidelity_b: Razer Opus Active Noise Cancelling ANC Wireless Headphones: THX Audio Tuning - 25 Hr Battery - Bluetooth 4.2 & 3.5mm Jack Compatible - Auto Play/Auto Pause - Carrying Case Included - Midnight Blue

Amazon Basics Party Speaker - Wireless PA Speaker with Lights, Radio, Bass Boost, Mic Input and USB Charging ***Updated** 8/13/2019

This speaker was plugged in and fully charged after receiving. I have not been able to get it to charge since. Even when plugged in it turns on, says low battery then immediately turns off.

I removed battery to manually charge (there is a compartment under the speaker). Once removed from charger at 26v, as soon as it was connected to the stereo, voltage dropped to 10v, said low battery again and shut off. This speaker went straight to the trash. I had higher hopes for this speaker. Unfortunately it didn’t last longer than a couple of weeks.

For the size of this speaker, I was expecting much better sound.

With the bass button on, the sound is fairly clear and sounds ok. Bass doesn’t hit as hard as I thought it would. I have another speaker half the size that sounds better than this one (at half the price). Without the bass button turned on, the sound is much lower and no longer allows an equalizer setting to be selected.

To turn on, press and hold power button. BT setup was easy and device will automatically connect to the last paired device upon turning on.

Once charged, this is a wireless speaker. It can be paired to another identical speaker. I don’t need 2 of these so I won’t be doing that. It would be nice if it could be paired to any other BT capable speaker.

There are handles on the sides to make carrying easy.

USB port is convenient for charging your phone or other mp3 device. Microphone port works fine and has its own volume knob.

The light on the speaker isn’t super bright but is annoying during daylight hours. It comes on automatically after the bass button is pressed and has to be manually shut off by pressing the light button 7-8 times (it has to go through each of the light settings before turning off).

This would be alright as a garage speaker or even as a kids karaoke machine but It isn’t something I would want to carry around to parties, nor is the sound something to show off.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics Party Speaker - Wireless PA Speaker with Lights, Radio, Bass Boost, Mic Input and USB Charging

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Touch, Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display I have unusual needs for the Kindle Touch. It is my study device. As an autodidact moving along in years I found that lugging a lot of textbooks/reference books/dictionaries around was getting in the way of learning. Sure, I can use a laptop for lots of online material to study but when I'm comfortable in my easy chair and the laptop is in the other room I just don't want to get up. Enter the Touch. I am reading philosophy and studying Latin on my own. I have loaded the Touch up with many free or low cost books on Aristotle and St. Thomas Aquinas. I have many personal Latin documents, some Latin readers and texts, Interlinear translation of the Douay-Rheims Bible, etc. Now I discover that I can save web pages in html file format and convert them to mobi format for the Touch and end up with "live" links to hundreds of web pages I am interested in using in my studies. I have sent these documents to the Touch either using the email forwarding capability or the conversion program directly(Calibre-free download. A terrific program recommended by a Kindle Touch tech services guy. Wouldn't be without it!) The Kindle Touch when hooked to my home wireless network downloads web pages very fast. I can look up anything I need on Latin grammar from the web and even bookmark pages I want to save for later use. If I'm out and about I can find any free Wi Fi location and log on and do the same.

The things that are invaluable and a couple are unique to the Touch--the Fire, or the iPad 3 cannot do them, are:

1. Change the default dictionary to Latin, or any language for which you can get a digital dictionary that works with Kindle Touch. I have two Latin dictionaries that cost nearly nothing! This is a great help to anyone trying to translate and learn a new language. If I can't find it in the default ditionary I am using I then work the magic of...............

2. Web search for Latin words. I can get Google Translate, the Whitaker Latin Dictionary, Perseus Latin Word Search, etc through the browser. Pages I want to use often I can Bookmark and open them through the Menu screen for the Touch. Then, and this is crucial...........

3. You can expand browser pages by a couple of taps or by the expanding finger touch move on the screen. Many Latin words are displayed in tables that are actually images and are really too small to deal with. Just hold your finger/stylus on the screen, the box pops up and the little magnifying glass with + sign in it appears. Press that and Voila! the image now fills the screen in comfortable text size. This can be done with books too and makes tables of conjugated verbs, noun declensions etc from texts and web pages super readable and thus useful.

4. Notes. Press an word that I want to look up later, type a note about my thought(s) or that I want to translate off the web later on, save it and then look up later in View Notes and Marks for the document/book I am working with. A great way to study!

5. The reading screen is so comfortable to use. Absolutely no glare and I cannot say that about Kindle Fire or iPads--anti-glare covers are a necessity with them. Just try to read something with the Fire on sunny day while sitting in the car waiting for your spouse to get finished shopping. Not easy. With the Touch it is simplicity in itself. Just turn on and read.

6. Many books have an interactive "live" table of contents. If I really want that in a book I download a sample first and check. If it doesn't have one I may not buy although you can navigate with page/location numbers if necessary. Just a bit more awkward.

7. Amount of stuff on the device. I have over 4000 pages of the works of St. Thomas Aquinas, Aristotle's complete works of his major writings, again nearly 1000 pages, several very large Latin textbooks, other philosophy books, three different copies of the Bible, etc etc. Probably approaching 7-8000 pages of material ALL AT MY FINGERTIPS!........Plus the web when near Wi Fi and connected.

My wife received her Touch from me for her birthday. She is a voracious reader of thriller/mystery novels, the Vince Flynn, David Baldacci, et. al., genre. Since she got the Kindle Touch her reading speed has increased noticeably. She can make the type as large as she wants it to be, adjust the interlinear gap and look up words she doesn't know with the default English dictionary that comes with the device.

Finally, I can charge my Touch, use it everyday, web time, download time, reading time and a lot of just looking at the screen "think time" I charge it about every two weeks. She does the same, maybe less frequently because she doesn't make the Internet demands on her device that I do on mine. The Fire or the iPad--admittedly devices with much more capability for complex displays, videos, etc can make 7-10 hours before a charge is required. That can be a problem for people on the move.

I am sure I will find other great uses for this device. So far, I can find no knocks at all. My wife had to exchange her first machine because the touch screen wasn't quite right. That was a snap. I have contacted Kindle Customer/Technical Service Support about 7-8 times with questions or wanting to return her first device(which was replaced with the new one by overnight shipment!!!!!!!!!!! At no charge. Had the new one before we had to send the old one back. That is customer service.) The people I have talked to are well-trained, smart, very easy to talk to and polite beyond my experience on the web. Amazon customer service is superior. That is a major selling point as well.

I do not work for Amazon, never heard of them until a few years ago and nobody has helped me learn to use my Touch or my wife's either beyond a few calls about things that were actually easy to take care of if I had only read the right page of the manual. I would buy Touch again in a second! At $99 for the one with ads, which I have, or my wife's without ads at $139 there is not better reading/study device available outside of a full-fledged laptop/desktop computer, and I hate to sit in front of them all day anyhow.

Thank you Amazon. You have scored 10+
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Touch, Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display

text_fidelity_a:
Winegard HD8200U Platinum VHF/UHF HDTV Antenna (65 Miles+, Digital, 4K Ultra High-Def Ready) First, be aware this beast is more than 14 feet long and about 9 feet wide when unfolded and assembled. It does move in the wind. It doesn't weigh that much, but with so many elements forming such a large device it becomes a sail.

I mounted it on a 10' length of 1-1/4" electrical conduit held to a tall garage wall using [[ASIN:B001RCMEEA Channel Master CM-9025 3-Inch Heavy-Duty Wall Mount for TV Antenna Masts]]. The antenna is about 23 feet in the air.

The HD8200U has a very high-gain, directional Yagi UHF antenna on the front and a full VHF antenna on the rear. I really don't think I need the VHF section and may retire this antenna and opt for a more compact UHF Yagi if the high winds we occasionally experience cause trouble. After assembly, the two sections feed into an electronics box using 1/8" aluminum rods from each section. You then mechanically attach a top plate to the box that connects to all four aluminum leads. The coax connector is in this top plate. A weather boot is supplied to seal the connection.

The HD8200U does bring in the signal like a champ. My stations are at least 19 miles and 68 miles away. It's very directional. If I aimed 30 degrees off, I got zero channels. Check where your stations are broadcast from using www.antennaweb.org (antennaweb dot org) which provides distance and direction in degrees from magnetic north using your zip code. Very handy.
text_fidelity_b: Winegard HD8200U Platinum VHF/UHF HDTV Antenna (65 Miles+, Digital, 4K Ultra High-Def Ready)
